Fervent

FUR-vunt -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, FUR. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fervent is having passionate intensity.

She made a fervent promise at her grandfather's bedside to finish the field guide he had started.

Worked Example

At the vigil for the missing fishing crew, nobody shouts and nobody cheers. But the waterfront is packed shoulder to shoulder, candles steady against the wind, every quiet voice burning with the same fervent hope.

Fervent means having passionate intensity -- feeling that burns hot. Notice that nothing here is cheerful: fervent works for solemn wishes, urgent prayers, and deep beliefs just as well as for joyful causes. The heat of the feeling, not happiness, is the point.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wholehearted: complete and without any doubts

intense: very strong in degree or force

passionate: driven by powerful feeling

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lukewarm: without real interest or energy

detached: emotionally uninvolved

Where it sits · how much heat the feeling carries — wholehearted → fervent → passionate

wholehearted vs. fervent: Wholehearted says all of you agrees -- wholehearted support has no doubts in it -- while fervent adds heat: the support does not just fill you, it burns.

passionate vs. fervent: Passionate is the closest and strongest partner: both blaze, but passionate can describe a person's whole nature, while fervent usually attaches to one feeling aimed at one thing -- a fervent hope, a fervent belief, a fervent plea.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ferv-

root — ferv-: to boil, to glow (Latin fervere)

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: being in a state of (Latin -entem)

Put it together

Put it together: Fervent comes from Latin fervere, 'to boil.' Fervent feeling is feeling at a boil -- hot, intense, and impossible to mistake for lukewarm politeness, whether the feeling is joyful, hopeful, or solemn in the most serious way.

Use the root in a new word: effervescent

Use the root in a new word: effervescent: The effervescent cider fizzed over the rim of the glass.

Root Check

Word Choice

Fervent measures the temperature of a feeling, not its cheerfulness: a fervent hope at a hospital bedside is as natural as fervent cheering at a parade. Keep it apart from ardent, its nearest neighbor: fervent describes how hot the feeling burns, while ardent describes devotion -- loyalty aimed at a team, a cause, or a person. The ISEE loves that hairline: a fervent prayer, an ardent fan.
